# The Value of Disagreement: Why Good Meetings Don't End in Consensus

## The Consensus Trap

There's a moment near the end of many meetings that feels like success. Someone looks around the table, sees heads nodding, and declares, "Great, so we're all aligned." People file out satisfied. The meeting worked. Everyone agreed.

But did they? Often, what looks like agreement is actually a kind of collective fog. People nod for different reasons: because they're tired, because they don't want to be the difficult one, because they genuinely believe they agree but are using the same words to mean different things, or because they're deferring to whoever spoke most confidently. The meeting ends, everyone walks away with a slightly different picture of what was decided, and three weeks later the project stalls while two people discover they were never actually on the same page.

This is the quiet failure of consensus. When a group converges too quickly on a shared conclusion, it may have found the truth—or it may have simply suppressed the differences that would have revealed the truth. The problem is that from the outside, these two situations look identical. A room full of nodding heads tells you nothing about whether the group has converged on something real.
